chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Numbers That Drive Value

lessons.title: Revenue, EBITDA, PAT and Free Cash Flow: What Valuers Actually Look At

children.text: Hand a valuer your annual accounts and watch what they do. They will not read every line. They will pull out four numbers, in a fixed order, and most of their questions will be about the distance between them. Learn to read that same ladder and you can follow any valuation conversation in the building.

body.text: Revenue tells you how big you are. EBITDA tells you what the operations earn. Profit after tax tells you what is left for shareholders. Free cash flow tells you what actually reached the bank account. Only the last one pays salaries, dividends or a loan instalment.

children.text: The Ladder from Revenue to Profit

cells: Revenue
Sales of goods and services, net of returns and discounts
Every cost. A company can grow revenue while burning cash on each order
EBITDA
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation
The cost of the assets used, the cost of debt and tax
EBIT
EBITDA after depreciation and amortisation. Also called operating profit
Interest and tax
PBT
Profit before tax, after interest and other income
Tax
PAT
Profit after tax, the bottom line attributable to shareholders
Cash actually spent on new assets and stuck in working capital

children.text: The gap between EBITDA and EBIT is
depreciation and amortisation

and it is where asset-heavy businesses differ from asset-light ones. The gap between EBIT and PAT is interest and tax, which is where two companies with identical operations but different borrowings part company.

markDefs.definition: The annual accounting charge that spreads the cost of an asset over its useful life. It is a real cost of doing business, but it involves no cash payment in the year it is charged.

children.text: Worked Example: Konkan Ceramics
Konkan Ceramics Private Limited is a fictional Ratnagiri tile maker. Here is its FY26 profit and loss account, in ₹ crore, with a 25% tax rate.

cells: Revenue
Tiles sold during the year
Less: operating costs
Clay, power, factory wages, freight, selling and admin costs
EBITDA
Less: depreciation and amortisation
The kiln and factory written down over their useful lives
EBIT (operating profit)
Less: interest
On the term loan for the kiln
PBT
Less: tax at 25%
PAT

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: how ₹200 crore of revenue becomes ₹15 crore of profit
body.xAxisLabel: Line in the profit and loss account

body.title: A new kiln changes the picture
body.prompt: Konkan commissions a second kiln, and depreciation for the year rises from ₹12 crore to ₹18 crore. Nothing else changes: EBITDA stays at ₹40 crore, interest at ₹8 crore and tax at 25%. What is PAT now, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: EBIT = ₹40 crore - ₹18 crore = ₹22 crore. PBT = ₹22 crore - ₹8 crore = ₹14 crore. Tax at 25% is ₹3.5 crore, so PAT = ₹10.5 crore. EBITDA did not move at all, which is exactly why a buyer of an asset-heavy business should never look at EBITDA alone.

The mechanics do not change with size. Tata Consultancy Services reported these figures for the year ended March 2025.

stats.label: Operating margin
stats.context: Which puts operating profit at roughly ₹62,044 crore

stats.label: Profit before tax
stats.context: Higher than operating profit because of other income

body.title: Two things you can work out from those four numbers

children.text: First, the effective tax rate.

content.caption: Tax paid as a share of profit before tax, in ₹ crore

children.text: Second, notice that profit before tax (₹65,331 crore) exceeds operating profit (about ₹62,044 crore). For an operating company that usually means other income, most often interest and gains on a large pile of invested cash. A valuer separates that from the operating business, because income on surplus cash is not something the IT services operation generates.

content.text: This is a habit worth building. Every time two numbers in a set do not line up in the direction you expect, there is a story in the gap, and the gap is usually where the valuation argument lives.

children.text: Why Valuers Reach for EBITDA, and Where It Misleads

EBITDA is popular for one good reason: it strips out financing and tax, so two companies running the same operations look comparable even if one is loaded with debt and the other is not. That makes it useful for comparing businesses. It also makes it dangerous.

body.title: EBITDA: the case for and against

columns.label: What EBITDA does well
points: Compares operating performance across companies with different debt levels
Removes distortions from different tax positions and past asset purchases
Is the base for the EV/EBITDA multiple used in most mid-market Indian deals
Is harder to manage through depreciation policy than PAT is

columns.label: What EBITDA hides
points: Capital expenditure, which is very real for factories, trucks and data centres
Working capital stuck in inventory and receivables
Interest, which must be paid whether or not profits arrive
Tax, which is not optional either

children.text: Vodafone Idea shows the gap at full scale. In the quarter ended March 2025 the company reported gross revenue of about ₹11,014 crore and EBITDA of about ₹4,659 crore. It also reported finance costs of about ₹6,471 crore and a net loss of about ₹7,166 crore for the same quarter.

body.label: Vodafone Idea, quarter ended March 2025
body.context: Interest alone (about ₹6,471 crore) was larger than the entire quarter's EBITDA. Subtract it and you are already at roughly minus ₹1,812 crore, and the distance from there to the reported loss of about ₹7,166 crore, some ₹5,354 crore, is largely depreciation and amortisation on a telecom network. A positive EBITDA told you almost nothing about whether this business could pay its bills.

body.text: When a founder or a banker quotes only EBITDA, ask the next three questions immediately. How much capital expenditure does the business need each year just to keep running? How much cash is tied up in working capital? What does it pay in interest?

children.text: Profit Is an Opinion, Cash Is a Fact

PAT is an accounting result. It records sales when invoiced, not when collected, and it charges depreciation for assets bought years ago while ignoring the cash paid for a new machine this year. Free cash flow corrects for all of that.

body.caption: Free cash flow to the firm, the number a DCF actually discounts. t is the tax rate

children.text: Run Konkan Ceramics through it. EBIT is ₹28 crore, so after tax at 25% that is ₹21 crore. Add back the ₹12 crore of depreciation, because no cash left the company for it. Then subtract the ₹20 crore spent on the new kiln and the ₹8 crore of extra cash swallowed by higher inventory and customer credit.

body.caption: Konkan Ceramics: from operating profit to free cash flow (₹ crore)

cells: EBIT after tax (₹28 crore × 0.75)
Add back depreciation and amortisation
Less capital expenditure on the new kiln
Less increase in working capital
Free cash flow

body.text: PAT said ₹15 crore. Free cash flow said ₹5 crore. Both are correct. The ₹10 crore difference is a kiln and a warehouse full of tiles, and it is the reason profitable Indian companies still run out of cash.

body.title: A year without the kiln
body.prompt: In the following year Konkan spends only ₹10 crore of capital expenditure. EBIT is still ₹28 crore, tax 25%, depreciation ₹12 crore and the working capital increase ₹8 crore. What is free cash flow, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹21 crore + ₹12 crore - ₹10 crore - ₹8 crore = ₹15 crore. Cut capital expenditure and cash flow jumps, which is why buyers always ask how much of the capital expenditure is maintenance the business cannot avoid and how much is growth it can pause.

children.text: Normalisation: The Numbers a Valuer Rebuilds

In Indian private companies, reported profit rarely equals sustainable profit. Before applying any multiple, a valuer normalises the accounts by adding back what a new owner would not incur and removing what will not repeat.

cells: Promoter remuneration far above or below market
Reset to a market salary for the role
A buyer will have to pay a professional manager the market rate
Rent paid to a family-owned property firm
Restate to market rent
The related-party rate is a shareholder decision, not a business cost
Personal expenses routed through the company
Add back
They will not continue after a sale
A one-off legal settlement or insurance claim
Remove from the year it appears in
It says nothing about next year's earnings
Government incentive that has now ended
Remove
Future buyers cannot count on it

body.title: What to ask for before trusting an EBITDA figure
steps: Audited financial statements for the last three years, not just management accounts
A schedule of every normalisation adjustment, with the amount and the reason
Related-party transactions: rent, salaries, loans and purchases
Capital expenditure for the last three years, split between maintenance and growth
Working capital by month, so seasonal swings are visible
The cash flow statement, read alongside the profit and loss account

children.text: Which Number for Which Job

body.caption: Matching the metric to the situation

cells: An early-stage or loss-making company
Revenue, with a revenue multiple
There is no profit to multiply yet
A mature private company in a deal
Normalised EBITDA, with an EV/EBITDA multiple
Comparable across different debt and tax positions
Comparing listed companies on NSE or BSE
PAT, through the P/E ratio
Earnings per share is what listed investors are buying
A DCF valuation
Free cash flow
It is the only figure that represents cash available to investors
A bank assessing a loan
EBITDA against interest and repayments
It tests whether operations can service the debt

body.title: Comparing across balance sheets
body.question: You are comparing two identical-looking cement companies. One is debt free, the other has borrowed heavily to build its plants. Which metric lets you compare their operating performance most fairly?
options: Profit after tax, since it is the bottom line
EBITDA, since it sits above interest and tax
Revenue, since it is unaffected by accounting choices
Earnings per share, since it is per share
body.explanation: Interest on the borrowings will crush the leveraged company's PAT and EPS even if both plants run identically well. EBITDA sits above interest and tax, so it compares the operations themselves. You then bring the debt back in when you convert enterprise value to equity value, which Lesson 3.2 covers.

body.title: Signing off on a deal model
body.scenario: You run operations at a listed logistics group. The corporate development team circulates a model for acquiring a cold chain business, valuing it at 9 times EBITDA of ₹60 crore, or ₹540 crore. The target's reefer trucks are on average seven years old, and the model assumes capital expenditure of ₹15 crore a year for the next five years. Depreciation in the target's accounts runs at ₹48 crore a year.
body.prompt: You are asked for comments before the offer goes out. What do you raise?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The capital expenditure assumption contradicts the depreciation. Charging ₹48 crore of depreciation while assuming ₹15 crore of spending implies the fleet shrinks in value every year. For a seven year old reefer fleet, replacement spending is likely to be far closer to the depreciation figure.
2. Ask for maintenance capital expenditure separately from growth capital expenditure, with the fleet replacement schedule behind it.
3. Ask what the ₹60 crore EBITDA looks like after normalisation. Promoter salaries, related-party workshop charges and any one-off contract gains should be stripped out.
4. Ask for the free cash flow, not the EBITDA. At 9 times EBITDA we are paying ₹540 crore for a business whose cash generation after real capital expenditure may be a fraction of ₹60 crore.
5. Check working capital. Logistics contracts with large corporates often carry 60 to 90 day payment terms, and that cash requirement grows with revenue.
6. Sanity check the multiple itself against recent deals in Indian logistics, and against what our own listed group trades at. Paying a higher multiple than our own only makes sense if the business grows faster or brings genuine synergies.

body.title: The add-back
body.textWithBlank: When moving from operating profit to free cash flow, depreciation is added back because it is a cost that involves no ___ outflow in the year it is charged.
body.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset bought earlier. The cash left the company when the asset was purchased, which is why capital expenditure is subtracted separately.

body.label: Screener.in: Tata Consultancy Services
body.description: Open the profit and loss tab and walk down the ladder yourself: sales, operating profit, depreciation, interest, profit before tax and net profit. Then open the cash flow tab and compare net profit with cash from operations.

cards.definition: Sales for the period, before any costs. A measure of size, not of success.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Operating performance before financing and asset costs.
EBITDA less depreciation and amortisation. Also called operating profit.
Profit after tax. What is left for shareholders in the accounts, not in the bank.
EBIT after tax, plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and the increase in working capital.
Adjusting reported profit for one-off and non-business items to find sustainable earnings.
The spending needed just to keep the existing business running at its current level.

points: Valuers read a fixed ladder: revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, PBT, PAT. The interesting questions live in the gaps between the rungs.
Depreciation separates asset-heavy from asset-light businesses. Konkan Ceramics kept EBITDA at ₹40 crore while PAT fell from ₹15 crore to ₹10.5 crore purely on a new kiln.
EBITDA compares operations across different debt levels, which is useful, but it ignores capex, working capital, interest and tax.
Vodafone Idea reported about ₹4,659 crore of EBITDA and a loss of about ₹7,166 crore in a single quarter. Positive EBITDA is not a sign of health.
Free cash flow is what a DCF discounts: EBIT after tax, plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and the working capital increase.
Reported profit in a private company is rarely sustainable profit. Normalisation adjustments come before any multiple is applied.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Konkan Ceramics and the cold chain target are fictional. Figures for TCS and Vodafone Idea are taken from published results for the periods stated, and the depreciation figure inferred for Vodafone Idea is an arithmetical gap, not a reported line item. Always work from the audited financial statements themselves.
